original_value: Icebergs and ice islands (large, tabular icebergs) are challenging targets to survey due to their size, mobility, remote locations, and potentially difficult environmental conditions. Here, we assess the precision and utility of aerial photography surveying with structure-from-motion multi-view stereo photogrammetry processing (SfM) and vessel-based terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) for iceberg deterioration detection and mass estimation. For both techniques, we determine the minimum amount of change required to reliably resolve iceberg deterioration, the deterioration detection threshold (DDT), using triplicate surveys of two iceberg survey targets. We also calculate their relative uncertainties for iceberg mass estimation. The quality of deployed Global Positioning System (GPS) units that were used for drift correction and scale assignment was a major determinant of point cloud precision. When dual-frequency GPS receivers were deployed, DDT values of 2.5 and 0.40 m were calculated for the TLS and SfM point clouds, respectively. In contrast, values of 6.6 and 3.4 m were calculated when tracking beacons with lower-quality GPS were used. The SfM dataset was also more precise when used for iceberg mass estimation, and we recommend further development of this technique for iceberg-related end-uses.

result.paraphrase: Icebergs and ice islands, which are large tabular icebergs, are difficult to survey because of their size, mobility, remote locations, and sometimes harsh environmental conditions. In this study, we evaluate the accuracy and usefulness of aerial photography surveying processed with structure-from-motion multi-view stereo photogrammetry (SfM) and vessel-based terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) for detecting iceberg deterioration and estimating mass. Using triplicate surveys of two iceberg targets, we determine for both methods the minimum change needed to reliably identify deterioration, or the deterioration detection threshold (DDT). We also compute the relative uncertainties in iceberg mass estimates. Point cloud precision depended heavily on the quality of the deployed Global Positioning System (GPS) units used for drift correction and scale assignment. With dual-frequency GPS receivers, DDT values of 2.5 m and 0.40 m were obtained for the TLS and SfM point clouds, respectively. By contrast, when tracking beacons with lower-quality GPS were used, the values were 6.6 m and 3.4 m. The SfM dataset was also more precise for estimating iceberg mass, and we recommend continued development of this technique for iceberg applications.
